title: Give what you command (10.29)
hook: everyone says you've got this; Augustine prays for the strength being asked of him, and a teacher in Rome can't bear it
tomorrow: you know what time is, until someone asks. so what is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's late love: God called, then shouted, and got through. The line was you broke my deafness. Now he's listening, and he asks for something.

Everyone says you've got this. The coach, the group chat, the card from your aunt. And some nights the honest answer is: not on my own. Augustine wrote a sentence for that night, and it started a fight. Rome. A bishop is reading Augustine's words aloud to a room. A visiting teacher named Pelagius is listening, and his face changes. Augustine later wrote that Pelagius couldn't bear those words, and argued against them so hotly he nearly quarreled with the bishop who quoted them. All that, over one short sentence from a prayer in the middle of a book.
screen: `YOU'VE GOT THIS. DO YOU?` → `A BISHOP READS IT ALOUD IN ROME.` → `PELAGIUS CAN'T BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence. Book ten of the Confessions is Augustine, now a bishop, taking inventory. Not who he was, but who he still is: the pull of food, of lovely things, of praise. He doesn't pretend he's finished. He says all his hope is in God's great mercy, and then he prays, in the Pusey translation: "Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt." In plain words: give what you command, and command what you like. Read it slowly and it's two requests. The second is surrender: ask anything of me. The first is the honest part: I can't do this alone, so give me the very thing you ask. Pelagius heard danger. He wanted people to take their own effort seriously, and the prayer sounded to him like permission to sit back. Augustine's answer was that grace doesn't replace the effort. Grace is what makes the effort possible. Catholic teaching keeps both halves. The Catechism says even getting ready to receive grace is already the work of grace. And here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Catechism quotes Augustine himself, that God created us without us, but did not will to save us without us.
screen: `BOOK TEN: TAKING INVENTORY.` · `TWO REQUESTS IN ONE LINE.` · `PELAGIUS HEARD AN EXCUSE.` · `GRACE, AND NOT WITHOUT US.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU ASK.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write one thing being asked of you right now: patience with someone, an honest word, the job you keep dodging. Under it, write where your own strength runs short. If you pray, read both lines back slowly, then Augustine's: give what you command, and command what you will.
Give what you command. Augustine's prayer in book ten: asking God for the very strength God asks of you.
Keep this one: give what you ask, with empty hands that are still ready to work. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1457 COUNTS.` → `CONFESSIONS · 31 OF 35.` → `TOMORROW: YOU KNOW WHAT TIME IS, UNTIL SOMEONE ASKS. SO WHAT IS IT?`

howItsDone: Catholics ask God for grace before hard tasks, in their own words or with lines from the saints. The Church teaches that grace comes first and that human freedom and effort still take part.

fork.setup: a friend starts a new job she's sure she'll fail. she says, "i'm praying about it, so i don't need to prepare." what does Augustine's line suggest?
options: ask for the strength, and prepare anyway: grace makes the work possible.
she's right: if God gives what he commands, preparing shows doubt.
skip the prayer and just prepare; it all depends on her.
fork.reveal: Augustine prayed give what you command, and still answered Pelagius that effort matters. Catholic teaching keeps both: grace first, and not without us.

chat.meaning: Give what you command asks God for the strength his call needs. Grace doesn't replace effort; Augustine says it makes effort possible.

Augustine.meaning: the North African bishop who wrote the Confessions

Pelagius.meaning: a teacher who stressed human effort and argued with Augustine

Confessions.meaning: Augustine's life story, told as a prayer to God

Pusey.meaning: the translator of the Confessions used on this path

Catechism.meaning: the Catholic Church's summary of its teaching
